newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee steady, London seen gaining.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee steady, London seen gaining.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices were stable on Monday, with supply staying ample despite talk of lower production, traders said.

They said grade four Robusta was quoted at 3,200 rupiah/kg in Lampung, capital of the key growing region of South Sumatra, unchanged from last Friday's level. The export price was quoted at $1,400-$1,410/tonne, up from $1,400.
The traders said they expected London May futures to open $20 higher later on Monday.
"The market is active following gains in London on Friday, with buyers looking for beans," one trader said.

London's May and benchmark July contracts each finished $20 higher at $1,640 and $1,663 respectively on Friday. May was capped through the day at $1,650 a tonne on origin hedge selling, especially from Indonesia, London traders said.
"I expect London to open by about $20 higher following increases in New York later on Friday," one trader said.
Traders said supply remained ample in the local market despite talk of lower production this year, but added that the squeeze could come towards the end of the year.
"I am expecting supply to be tight from September onwards because of the production shortfall," one trader said.
"But at the moment, there is nothing to indicate that we might see a big drop in production this year," he added.

Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters, said in early April the country's production was expected to fall by some 30 percent this year from an original forecast of 480,000 tonnes due to bad weather. He said the total exportable volume would amount to 220,000 tonnes.
Another trader said some players were beginning to hold back sales in anticipation of better prices, but added that the situation was unlikely to stretch into the long-term.
"There are many things to consider such as cash flow and high interest rates," he said.
The trader said there had been talk of defaults in shipments of Arabica coffee from Indonesia totalling several hundred tonnes, and that the issue had yet to be resolved.

"Some sellers are believed to have entered into contracts when Arabica was around 3,000-4,000 rupiah and were caught when prices suddenly shot up," he said, adding that Arabica was being quoted locally at above 8,000 rupiah/kg.
"The sellers would have lost a lot of money if they had to meet the shipments," the trader said. "As I know it, the matter is still pending despite complaints from the buyers."
